extracted.intended_audience: general readers, television/comedy fans, and television history researchers
extracted.subtask_description: Describes the format, production practices, casting, and distribution of The Dean Martin Celebrity Roast TV specials (1974–1984), useful as a reference for producing or analyzing roast-style variety television. Focuses on structure of an episode, typical participants, taping/location practices, and home-media/syndication notes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Episode structure: introduction, roasters, honoree reply
rubrics_metrics.description: Every roast began with an introduction by roastmaster Martin, with jokes about the celebrity in question. He would then introduce each member of the dais, who would take turns adding insults or jokes about the honoree. In the end, the honoree would have their chance to insult the roastmaster and members of the dais.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This sets the standard three-part flow for an episode: roastmaster opening, sequential roaster jabs, and a closing response from the honoree. Examples include Henry Fonda's line during Bette Davis' roast and the honoree's final opportunity to trade insults. Use of timing and turn-taking is implied; a producer may plan introductions and ordering of roasters accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dais seating and honorifics for the roastee
rubrics_metrics.description: The roastmaster (Martin), the roastee, and the roasters would be seated on a dais. The roastees were also referred to as "Man of the Hour", "Woman of the Hour", or "Man of the Week" in earlier episodes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Physical staging (a dais) and formal/affectionate honorifics are part of the roast aesthetic. Maintaining visible proximity of roastmaster, roastee, and roasters reinforces the convivial/insulting atmosphere and is a production design consideration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lineage and comedic style: patterned after Friars' Club roasts
rubrics_metrics.description: The roasts were patterned after the roasts held at the New York Friars' Club.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expect an exchange of affectionate insults, celebrity in-jokes, and a celebratory tone consistent with Friars' Club tradition. This historical model informs tone, acceptable limits of joking, and audience expectations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Flexibility in honoree selection and presentation (pairs, posthumous portrayals)
rubrics_metrics.description: In two instances, a pair of celebrities were roasted at the same time: Jack Klugman and Tony Randall, and Dan Rowan and Dick Martin. Only one person was honored posthumously, George Washington (portrayed by Jan Leighton).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The format can accommodate single or multiple honorees and even historical/posthumous honors via impersonation. Producers should plan content and scripting differently for paired roastees or portrayed figures (e.g., historical impersonation).

rubrics_metrics.name: Casting practice: primarily comedians with occasional unexpected participants
rubrics_metrics.description: While most of the participants were comedians known for their work in such events, occasionally unexpected participants would be featured, such as British pop singer Petula Clark who was recruited to help roast TV actor William Conrad in 1973.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Predominant reliance on professional comedians for roasts, but occasional cross-over casting (musicians, athletes, politicians) can add novelty. Casting choices affect the comedic style and audience reception.

rubrics_metrics.name: Production logistics: taping locations and segmented taping
rubrics_metrics.description: Starting with Bob Hope in 1974, the roast was taped in California and turned out to be a hit, leading to many other roasts to follow. In the fall of 1974, the roasts moved permanently to the MGM Grand Hotel's Ziegfeld Room in Las Vegas... Some segments were taped prior to or after the roast, due to considerations with the performer or technical aspects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Location (studio vs. hotel showroom) and segmented taping are standard production practices; logistical constraints (performer availability, technical needs) may require pre- or post-taping of parts of the episode. Producers should plan for site-specific staging and edit integration of separately taped segments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Episode branding: title varies with honoree
rubrics_metrics.description: The show's official title as a television special would change based on the celebrity; in James Stewart's case for instance, it would be the Dean Martin Celebrity Roast: Jimmy Stewart.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each special is branded around the honoree's name for promotional clarity. Marketing, credits, and packaging should reflect the featured celebrity prominently.

rubrics_metrics.name: Broadcasting pattern and running time
rubrics_metrics.description: For a series of 54 specials and shows, Martin and his friends would 'roast' a celebrity... The roasts mainly aired Thursdays on NBC. Running time: Varies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Roasts were treated as occasional specials rather than weekly episodes; runtime flexibility is acceptable. Scheduling as a special-event timeslot (e.g., Thursdays) affects promotion and expected audience size.

rubrics_metrics.name: Home media and rights considerations for releases
rubrics_metrics.description: The Dean Martin Celebrity Roasts were released on DVD through Guthy-Renker... NBC Universal brought suit against producer Greg Garrison and Guthy‑Renker for selling The Dean Martin Show DVDs; the suit did not affect the Celebrity Roasts. All 54 of the Celebrity Roasts are included in the 23-disc boxset Dean Martin Celebrity Roasts: Complete DVD Collection released October 15, 2013 by Time Life.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Commercial release requires clearances and can lead to rights disputes; packaging may combine related material selectively. Producers/distributors should secure necessary rights and be prepared for legal/clearance issues when assembling box sets or syndication packages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recurring performer practice and guest frequency
rubrics_metrics.description: Comedian Foster Brooks appeared the most often on the roast with each appearing 30 times. Michael Landon, Redd Foxx, Joe Namath, and Jack Klugman (with Tony Randall in 1973 and alone in 1978) were the only celebrities roasted twice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Shows often rely on a recurring stable of performers; repeat honorees are rare but possible. Understanding performer frequency helps in casting continuity and audience familiarity planning.
